Here's a long navel-gazing thread with my reactions:

I'm not a utilitarian and am generally suspicious of any overarching moral philosophy. But even in terms of overall utility, many people that practice weak EA do more good than few heroes that practice strong EA.

Second, empirically, EA has not only made it easier for people to allocate better the contributions that they would already have made, but also caused them to donate more. 

There are other movements that encourage people to give (e.g. religion) but EA appeals to different people

For same reason I'm not a longtermist, I think weak EA is important & good for helping people in need in the present.

Maybe you don't need a formula to figure out high-level goals, but you do need calculations to make interventions 20% more effective, and 20% is important.

Weak EA is where you decide to donate some small X% of your income to make the world better, and you allocate that by maximizing some concrete metric of utility. Michael quotes @amiasrinivasan's critique of weak EA  that it it's not radical enough, but doesn't mean it's not good

Strong EA is where you consider EA as an overarching moral philosophy that guides you in all aspects of your life, including what job to take, if to have kids, how to spent most of your resources. Most of @michael_nielsen 's critique only applies to strong EA.

3/5 Two examples:

text: 9/9 Finally, this is just an initial investigation. We think there are many more insights to be extracted, and invite you to play around with our webapp https://t.co/ctfH0Yl4oD . Upload your own images, and see how models' view of them evolves.

8/9 Pre-training significantly ameliorates such non monotonicity, and in general pre-trained models, even at same global accuracy, behave in much more consistent ways, that are more compatible with Bayesian models. See Section 5 of paper for more https://t.co/nFvkzR5IUS https://t.co/2J4JHau2ey

7/9 Also see barriers for theory, including "non Bayesian" behavior such as non monotonicity of accuracy & softmax entropy. In fact, we construct a CIFAR like dataset on which performance is *negatively correlated* with CIFAR performance. https://t.co/1s257lteVR

6/9 We take one step further and remove the distributions from "distribution shift". Surprisingly, can extract meaningful signal from a single point. By tracking evolution of accuracy & softmax probabilities as we increase resources, can see what&when models are learning. https://t.co/i2cqZz1kJL

5/9 Also, no standard statistical measure of distance can predict out-of-distribution performance of modern ML. 

E.g., ImageNet-R (renditions) is completely disjoint from ImageNet and yet Taori et al https://t.co/FoxkOXZwzu showed their performance is strongly correlated https://t.co/qzy8cymgfi

4/9 This doesn't make much sense in classical statistics. E.g you don't measure opinion polls by how well they predict Joe Smith's vote. But much of modern ML don't make sense from classical statistics viewpoint. Have you ever seen a US opinion poll pretrained on voters in China?

3/9 That is, we consider a collection of models parameterized by increasing resources such as compute (in this work) or data. Generally more resources = better *global* accuracy, but we track a single point's *profile*: how accuracy & softmax probabilities evolve with resources. https://t.co/Z0cPIeYmyq

2/9 Traditionally, ML classification/regression is considered a special case of statistical estimation. One measures performance of single empirical estimator with respect to population. In this paper we take dual approach: looking at single input wrt collection of estimators.

text:
@doschroeder @kennyog But I agree with broader point that the distinction between "theory" and "practice" is often meaningless. 
Certainly a single paper can contain contributions to both domains. Great practical works often teach us generalizable insights.
@doschroeder @kennyog The point I was making is that right now in deep learning, the dynamic is almost completely inverted.

@doschroeder @kennyog Examples include both multiparty secure computation and cold fusion. 

This classical view doesn't always hold, even in physics and crypto. Also, some people mix theory&practice (in a different universe, bitcoin could have been two papers: one on theory and one on implementation)

@doschroeder @kennyog Maybe the terms "ahead" or "behind" are not the right ones. I wanted to contrast a different dynamic between crypto in machine learning. The classical view of theory is that, because it's not tethered to practical considerations, it can move faster in exploring what's possible.

We want to come up with hypotheses clean enough to be informative, and precise enough to be refutable.

It is absolutely OK, as @tomgoldsteincs says, to be wrong. The danger we should watch out for is that we not become so vague in our hypotheses that we're "not even wrong".

So, if we want to gain understanding, mathematical theorems are one tool in our belt, but we can and should also reach for others, drawing inspiration from natural sciences.  These include not just theorems but also (and maybe mostly) observations and experiments.

..we have practical tools that exhibit too complex a behavior for us to analyze with our theoretical tools.

In that sense, these tools behave more similar to discovered natural objects than to designed algorithms.

They were proposed in 80s and 90s, considered wildly impractical, and only recently began to be implemented and used.

In contrast, in deep learning currently, practice is ahead of theory. Rather than having theoretical proposals that are too complex or inefficient to implement..

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I would guess that at the moment a large fraction, possibly a majority, of the Covid positive kids currently in isolation are both feeling fine and actually not infectious. Often by the time you get tested and get the results, much of the infectious period is over.

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I definitely agree that if you know for sure a kid *will* infect a classmate if they go to school then they should stay home. But often you could test positive (esp with PCR) at the tail end when you’re no longer infectious.

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I guess the question is reduces the chance by how much and what’s the conditional probability for a (vaxxed&boosted) kid to get sick of they do catch it. It seems the latter is lower for Covid than the flu.  I don’t know the answer to this calculation but it’s not obvious to me.

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I’m really sorry to hear that. I would have hoped that masking etc would at least keep kids from getting the flu. 

These respiratory diseases are all quite nasty, and I do hope that improved ventilation and more comfort with masks will reduce their prevalence in the future.

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias By “enforce” I mean that if kids are routinely tested even when not symptomatic, and then isolated if positive, then it should be done in most work places.

Otherwise the in-school transmissions we prevent will be drop in bucket of community transmissions

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias Maybe in the long run we can use rapid tests also for flu, and if you are actually infectious then you stay home. But we shouldn’t selectively enforce it for schools while everything else is open. Not just because it’s unfair but also because it’s pointless.

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias I think the Covid vaccine is actually more effective than the flu vaccine. Also masks do make a difference. If there is evidence that the risk from in-school infection is larger than community infection then isolation is worth it.

@JamesSurowiecki @mattyglesias Basically if new equilibrium is that large fraction of population will be exposed to Covid every year, might be better to focus on boosting&treatment rather than losing 5-10 days per exposure of school/work for people that feel fine.

13/14 I agree with this quote that access to math education *is* a social justice issue. But decreasing access to advanced math, and offering shallow alternative, will do nothing for equity. We need to do the work of reaching more students with quality math instruction. https://t.co/M9TXrkUlYK

12/14 STEM has become more mathematically sophisticated. You now see a gradient in every other CS talk, not to mention bra's, ket's, or elliptic curves. No one knows what math we'll need in future, but the best way to prepare students is to give broad & deep math foundation.

11/14 There is nothing special about "data science" that makes it more equitable. In fact, it is well known that it can replicate and amplify the biases that already exist in society. Data fluency is good, but making it is a solution to equity is magical thinking.

10/14 The CMF states that "the data science field provides opportunities for equitable practice, with multiple opportunities for students to pursue answers to wonderings and to accept the reality that all students can excel in data science fields."

9/14 The CMF itself describes skills in a high school data science class as "learn to clean data sets" "download and upload data" and develop something they call "data moves".

These vocational skills are no replacement to basic mathematical ways of thinking.

8/14 Am not against data science, but courses promoted by CA don't build lasting foundations, but rather teach to eyeball data and use spreadsheets & other tools that will likely be obsolete by the time students finish college.

Try to find an equation in https://t.co/6HCLtzzoRi

7/14 I am also not a "calculus fanatic" - I think probability,  discrete math, logic, can all be great ways to get math maturity needed for college STEM. But these topics are conceptually as hard or more as calculus. They do not require less math skills or preparation.

6/14 Same with initiatives such as the Algebra Project 
https://t.co/DVhXKRrkg7 or Calculus Project https://t.co/UZr3n0Flyn . All about "raising the floor" rather than lowering the ceiling. https://t.co/EAfwcaLizW

5/14 Some criticized CMF for introducing "social justice" to curricula. To the extent "Social Justice" is connecting students with math, I support it. (e.g. in @addiscoder, I used Abebech&Bruk instead of Alice&Bob)

What we *didn't do* in AddisCoder is water down content.

4/14 See blog for more, but some personal comments are in the thread below. These of course don't represent the other letter signers. 

I think the CMF authors are well-intentioned, and some of their proposals may be good, but on the whole their effect will be negative.

text: @jfitzsimons We know of course that if NP=P then we can break cryptography. The question is how would you demonstrate a function F in NP∩coNP (or AM∩coAM) such that you can break the encryption using F as an oracle. This should be a uniform function, not parameterized by public key.

20/20 Bottom line is that right now we do have candidates for post-quantum secure public-key encryption. But this could all change with a single algorithm, and we can't "rest easy" 

As I say in my survey, better understanding of PKE is urgent&important! 

https://t.co/8RbUorcvei

19/20 For more on relations of PKE and proof systems (SZK++) see the fascinating work of Berman et al 

https://t.co/51TZRCBUl9 https://t.co/mkzIC04LdJ

18/20 For such systems, distinguishing between fake&real public keys can be reduced to statistical distance and so they can be broken in  SZK ⊆ AM∩coAM.

However, other systems (including my own and McEliece) are not known to be broken in AM∩coAM.

17/20 In a public key system, if E0 and E1 are the distributions of encryptions of 0&1 respectively, they will be far. However in many lattice based systems one can generate a "fake public key" under which they are essentially identical (and decryption is impossible)

16/20 This is because the "statistical distance" problem is in SZK. This is the task of, given two randomized circuits E0&E1, of distinguishing between the case they induce statistically near and far distributions.

15/20 However, this assumes that we can recognize valid key/ciphertext pairs (e,c). This is the case for RSA but not necessarily for lattice based schemes. Still many lattice-based schemes can also be broken in NP∩coNP (or its cousin SZK ⊆ AM∩coAM).

14/20 As Goldreich-Goldwasser https://t.co/eEdvAKgsRu say, there is an old intuition from Brassard for (b) along following lines: if e is public-key and c is ciphertext, can certify that c is NOT an encryption of 1, by showing that it's an encryption of 0.
13/20 We have no evidence for (a), but let me also say why we don't know (b) either. ("We have no evidence" is not the same as "we have evidence that not"!)

12/20 However people are understandably worried whether there is something inherently incompatible between quantum computation and public-key encryption. In particular some in that thread suggested that maybe:
(a) NP∩coNP ⊆ BQP
(b) All PKEs can be broken in NP∩coNP

11/20 However:
1) Shor's algorithm doesn't affect private-key crypto.
2) We can construct public-key signatures based on private-key objects such as one-way functions or hash functions (though with cost in efficiency https://t.co/OJx86mvIyn). 
3) We still have lattices/coding!
10/20 Famously @PeterShor1 showed that quantum computers can break two out of the three main families of public-key encryption: factoring , discrete log, and lattice/coding.

9/20 People have looked at constructing other public-key encryptions, and I myself have proposed one (see https://t.co/tqoLY5s89P with Applebaum & Wigderson). But how secure these are and/or how different they are from others is still open question.

8/20 Essentially most constructions can be thought of as variants of either Diffie-Hellman, RSA, or Robert McEliece's system from 1978. The latter one is based on error correcting codes, and is related to other lattice/coding based systems. https://t.co/J4b7vny01l

7/20 The fact that these two independent lines stumbled across same constructions can be surprising, but in fact even 50 years later, we don't have that many more candidates for public key encryption schemes. 

https://t.co/8RbUorcvei https://t.co/1Fx0whLb8U

6/20 In late 1960's, James Ellis of British CESG had very similar thoughts https://t.co/vXbGRO01OZ. He realized PKE is not impossible, but didn't have a construction. First construction was by Cliford Cocks who "pre-discovered" RSA. Later Malcolm Williams pre-discovered D&H. https://t.co/u2Wm2JQDu5

5/20 Merkle, and Diffie&Hellman realized that PKE is not fundamentally impossible, but didn't know how it would be possible. Luckily, D&H got a great tip from their colleague John Gill to use modular exponentiation, which led to Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange https://t.co/grMCGIE3sh

4/20 When Berkeley undergraduate Ralph Merkle proposed it as a course project in 1974, it was rejected out of hand. When he submitted it to the CACM, the reviewer comments were that  “Experience shows that it is extremely dangerous to transmit key information in the clear.”

3/20 Public-key encryption is another beast altogether. First, its hard to overstate how revolutionary it was. Unlike heavier-than-air flight or many other inventions, despite cryptography's thousands year old history, PKE was not even *imagined*

2/20 Private key encryption often boils down to simply combining many non-local and non-linear operations. Making it efficient is challenging but if willing to lose some, a Monkey with a typewriter could probably construct a block cipher. See  https://t.co/rEW60HLVEl by @wtgowers

1/20 A 🧵 on public key cryptography, and its interaction with quantum computing. Spurred by a discussion w/ @jfitzsimons,  @mattyhoban, @dabacon, @rdviii but more general.

There is a fundamental gulf between public and private key encryption. https://t.co/ygixcwW3vq

https://t.co/QwdJjGclh3
16/21 Frankle's and co-authors works on understanding the efficient classifiers that are often "hidden in the belly" of more complex ones opens the door to making training & inference much cheaper.

15/21 Traditional "optimizing compilers" are bounded by (1) optimized code must be semantically equivalent and (2) most code is not perf bottleneck anyway. In contrast in ML (1) everything is approximate anyway and (2) training is hugely expensive.

14/21 Jonathan Frankle (https://t.co/8XqGbDIfVW @jefrankle) surprised the world of ML with his and advisor Carbin's "lottery ticket" paper. But his works extends far beyond. It exploits the fact that ML deals with *approximate computation* to get radically superior optimization

13/21 Some examples include learning perceptron under Massart noise https://t.co/IqhaIIgZ8z with extension to contextual bandits https://t.co/xudLyXBCcp  learning mixtures of product distributions https://t.co/79gnbajcov

12/21 Sitan Chen https://t.co/ilZBGkzNoE is problem-solver par excellence who worked on problems ranging from surpassing the 100+ years diffraction limit, classifying under adversarial noise, quantum state tomography, and more. Amazing theorist whose papers often come w/code

11/21 Morgane proved concentration theorems in "free probability" settings, replacing i.i.d. with certain "exchangability" conditions. To be honest, free probability is an area I'm deeply curious of but don't know much about so am excited to learn more from her!

10/21 Morgane Austern https://t.co/423GYAD8lG is joining Harvard statistics, but her work is relevant to computer scientists like me that care about concentration, especially in settings where traditional i.i.d assumptions don't hold.

9/21 In particular Anurag made great advances on "area laws" which show that for "natural" quantum states (arising from low dim geometries), the entanglement between two parts is bounded by their boundary. https://t.co/TSUNTUBLq7

8/21 Quantum mechanics are the foundations of our universe, and yet at large scale it always looks classical. Anurag Anshu (https://t.co/CNzn4Eq8nV , @AnuragAnshu4) works on understanding this puzzle, combining quantum many-body systems with constraint-satisfaction problems. https://t.co/0vj4KPDTVo
7/21 In addition to his work on OT, David is also a co-founder of the awesome RIIAA conference https://t.co/5OoW6Bx5Xc which brings together the Mexican and Latin-American AI communities.

6/21 Optimal transport is about mapping distribution X' to X while minimizing some distance. In particular OT allows using an algorithm designed for X on data coming from X'. This comes in handy if e.g. X is well-resourced language but X' is one with sparser data https://t.co/dh8Op9xCr1

5/21 Standard ML paradigm is datasets are few&big and algorithms many. But real life™ datasets often diverse&small. Hence tailoring data to algorithm might make more sense than other way around.

This is where David Alvarez-Melis' https://t.co/a1NaPjcVXS work comes in https://t.co/ku0r0zMX6o

@soashworth @beenwrekt First take on average-case analysis is often default clean distribution, such as random graphs, but then often people try to look at parameterized distribution (e.g., the probability of an edge), and then go to more sophisticated versions as well (eg stochastic block model).

4/ 4

To me, whether we view the generative models as corresponding to beliefs or to some approximation of how input was actually generated, is a second order consideration.

Once you are willing to assign probabilities in retrospect, you're not a frequentist anymore.

3/4

Bayesians are more "liberal" and are willing to accept "backward looking probabilities", where one is given a data and we retro-fit the generative model to the data.

This is the view behind average-case analysis of heuristics such as SAT solvers.

2/4 In such algorithm, we think of input as worst-case, and only randomness is over coins of algorithm which is completely under our control. 

This is in contrast to average-case analysis of algorithms (that can be randomized or deterministic)

1/4 Maybe answer deserves 🧵. My view is "frequentist" analysis holds probabilities to the highest standards. 

You can only talk about "forward-looking probabilities" in the sense that they are defined by first "pre-registering" an experiment, such as a randomized algorithm.

text: 12/12 Finally the 10 year award goes to Aaronson and Arkhipov's STOC 11 paper on Boson Sampling. Once again this is about the permanent. They show that the computational difficulty of sampling the permanent can be used to give evidence for quantum speedups! https://t.co/Vbnx28LsXV

11/12 Thorup and Zwick's paper studies the question of computing distances in large graph. Sure we can solve all pairs shortest paths, but that would require quadratic time. They showed a near-linear pre-processing that enables answering any distance query.

10/12 The first poly-time algorithm was Khachiyan's ellipsoid algorithm in 1979. It was & is much worse than simplex in practice, but it gave rise to interior point methods which can now often beat simplex on practical instances.

9/12 S&T gave a partial explanation by showing Simplex runs in poly-time if the inputs are perturbed, thereby initiating the field of smoothed analysis. 

Interestingly, for a long time it was not known if there is a poly-time algorithm for linear programming.

8/12 Spielman and Teng's work deals with one of best algorithmic stories of all times. The Simplex algorithm for linear programming was invented by Danzing in WW II. It's everyone's favorite example of an algorithm that is exponential in the worst case but efficient in practice. https://t.co/tKdQyQVHVo

7/12 Permanent is defined by a formula very similar to determinant except the absence of some -1 factors (see https://t.co/KGPPNvd1mg ) but unlike determinant, it's very hard to compute & even approximate. 

Paper shows difficulty almost disappears if matrix is non negative https://t.co/DDu4WOYl0s

6/12 20 year award goes to STOC 2001 papers of Jerrum-Sinclair-Vigoda, Spielman-Teng, and Thorup-Zwick.

Jerrum-Sinclair-Vigoda deals with one of TCS's favorite problems - the matrix permanent. It's a great example of the power and peril of negative numbers.

5/12 The STOC 88 & 89 papers above showed that we can obtain information-theoretically secure secure multiparty computation (MPC) if large enough fraction is honest. 

See @LindellYehuda's survey for more https://t.co/nJTJWVKSD5

4/12 What does this mean? That any collection of parties that do not trust each other, can still perform an arbitrary joint computation on their private inputs. 

This was established under assumptions by Yao & Goldreich-Micali-Wigderson. Surprisingly sometimes can do without!

3/12 These papers were part of the "crypto revolution" of the 1980s, when crypto extended beyond encryption & signatures to general protocol problems.

Arguably the fundamental theorem of cryptography is that we can simulate a virtual trusted third party.

(B) Representations learned with more data/compute should be better

5/7 Also show ∃ classical alg (implicit in  Aizenman, Lebowitz, and Ruelle 1987 and Lyons 2017) achieving 2/π≈0.63.  

While 0.63 < 0.71, interestingly in experiments, ALR algorithm often matches or beats QAOA even for locality>1 and graphs with small girth. https://t.co/aFrdKWzA9b

4/7 We show a limitation of 1-local quantum algorithms and an improved classical algorithm.

For D-regular high-girth graphs, any local alg outputs cut of value 1/2 + C/√D.   C can be at most Parisi constant ≈ 0.76. We show no 1-local quantum alg can achieve > 0.71. https://t.co/0sgcypxHd3

3/7 For given optimization problem, question is whether exists *any instance* where a quantum local alg such as QAOA beats all classical algs

text: 12/ I think that a society in which students are educated is a better one, and that along the way students get skills, and framework of knowledge  that make it easier for them to acquire new skills. I admit I have no proof for this, but employers & 100-year history seem to agree.

11/ Here I am biased. I think education is its own good, and it’s an inherent good for a student to see the proof of Godel’s Incompleteness Theorem, or understand the analysis of the multiplicative weights update method.

10/ To be sure - students actually do learn these topics in college. We do see how sophomores know more than first-years, and juniors more than sophomores. There is a reason courses have prerequisites. But is it “useful” for them to learn these topics?

9/ Not just “theory” topics such as Turing machines, halting problem and NP completeness. Whether it’s functional programming, designing recursive algorithms, writing assembler code by hand, or analyzing backpropagation, we routinely teach topics that 90% of developers don’t use.

8/ Finally, here is where @bryan_caplan is correct. People don’t use most of what they learn in high school & beyond.

Even in a supposedly “useful” major like computer science, I estimate that 90% of the time in their jobs, our graduates use less than 10% of topics we teach.

7/  If conscientiousness & conformity are traits that are important to an employer, these are traits that *can* be developed. It’s just that the army does a much better job developing them than universities.

6/ What is it that college signals? Caplan says it’s conscientiousness & conformity.

My wife is physical therapist that used to work a lot with the coast guard. Her patients always came 15 minutes early and were exceedingly polite.  My Harvard students? Not so much.

5/ Businesses can also take advantage without waiting for different policies. Most people don’t move far from their home. By placing your firm in areas with lower educational opportunities, you can find less educated workers that still have whatever it is that college “signals”

4/ There is simple policy prescription to take advantage of this inefficiency - a country that stops formal education at 8th grade & taxes/abolishes college, should get huge productivity boost. “Amazingly” countries with vastly varying cultures & regimes all doing the opposite.

3/ Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and this claim is indeed extraordinary. If Caplan is right then societies around the world are wasting 10-20% of people’s working years and hundreds of Billions of dollars for this useless signaling game.

2/ Caplan’s theory that about 80% of education beyond basic literacy and numeracy is just about “useless signaling”. It serves no useful purpose by itself. Rather students and employers get stuck in “arms race” of requiring ever more credentials to do jobs that don’t need them.

10/12

To get a sense, let's  consider baby case that data is X~N(0,I) and instead of clustering, algorithm outputs single set A and we want to bound P[ ‖μ(A)‖ ≥ θ | A].
Suppose μ(A)=v. We consider the one-dimensional affine subspace S = { X + αv⋅1_A for α∈ℝ }.

Reminiscent of differential-privacy based guarantees for safe hypothesis generation (@Aaroth & @mrtz can weigh in) but they consider deterministic clustering. Also also don't want to create new alg but analyze algs biologists already use & even give code (or at least R 😃)

8/12 

They consider clustering algorithms that take collection X of vectors and have some stability properties, in the sense that if you shift some subset of vectors by a small vector v, you will still get the same clustering.

7/12

This is what they want to do, and under assumptions, they manage to bound  P[ ‖ μ(A)−μ(B)‖ ≥ θ | clustering produces A,B  and more ] where "more" is additional conditions to make computation tractable.

6/12

Problem is that your clustering algorithm depends on the numbers, and conditioned on getting A and B, the p value that μ(A)-μ(B)>1.6 is actually large.
Arguably right thing is to compute P[ ‖ μ(A)−μ(B)‖ ≥ θ | clustering produces A,B ] .

5/12
But standard methods will tell you that with tiny p value, the two clusters really are different & you can (wrongly) rule out the null hypothesis that data is random numbers.

Happens also with single cell & even Penguins 😃 https://t.co/O5dhj3HPw7

4/12
Here is a simple example why things could go wrong. Imagine data is just 100 numbers from N(0,1),
and we partition it to two clusters A and B - the positive and negative numbers. Unsurprisingly, the mean of A will be about 1.6 larger than B's mean.

For both deep learning and SAT, most of time they succeed in tasks that humans can already do, but maybe on bigger scale. Deep learning usually used for human-doable tasks. SAT solvers often also prove theorems such as correctness of programs that humans could in principle do.

The possibility of P=NP is because there could be a "surprising" algorithm. If we knew that GD and friends were optimal, then there are no surprises, and we would actually be much closer to a "complete" theory of what's computationally feasible and not.

Counter take - the success of deep learning and SAT solvers is evidence for P≠NP and that maybe we actually understand algorithms better than we think

Why? Both deep learning and SAT solvers use local search algorithms. In particular easy to come up with hard instances for both

@GilKalai @quantum_aram @AspectStalence You are a brave man @GilKalai :)

Your goal as author is to ensure:

1) Beginning of paper clarifies what you did and why it’s important

2) Remainder shows reviewer you dotted your i’s and crossed your t’s and so they can trust you to have done thorough work in experiments, theory, and literature search.
I believe that often (not always!) by page 2 or so, the reviewer already knows if they want to accept or reject, and at this point are looking for more evidence to confirm this belief.

3) Know reader’s context - the only thing you can assume your reviewer knows is other papers in the same conference, so paper should be written to look like these papers. Reviewer has expectation to find things in Figure 1 etc

(Still struggling w this personally for ML papers)

1) “Front load” contributions - reader should get gist as early as possible. Should know result from abstract and why they should care by page 2.

2) No surprises - paper is not mystery novel - shouldn’t spring up important contributions, caveats or relevant prior work late.

Good advice, not just for ML. Some issues are fixable aspects of current review process, but many are inherent when you have reviewers with little time and limited experience.
